Colanode relies on **Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs)** - powered by Yjs - to allow real-time collaboration on entries like pages or database records. This means multiple people can edit at the same time, and the system gracefully merges everyone's updates. Deletions are also tracked as specialized transactions. Messages and file operations don't support concurrent edits and use simpler database tables.

The easiest way to start using Colanode is through our **web app**, accessible instantly at app.colanode.com. Simply log in to get started immediately, without any installation. _Please note, the web app is currently in early preview and under testing; you may encounter bugs or compatibility issues in certain browsers._
For optimal performance, you can install our **desktop app**, available from our downloads page. Both the web and desktop apps allow you to connect to any of our free beta cloud servers:

If you prefer to host your own Colanode server, check out the `hosting/` folder which contains the Docker Compose file and deployment configurations. For Kubernetes deployments, see the `hosting/kubernetes/` folder which includes Helm charts and additional documentation. Here's what you need to run Colanode yourself:
1. Copy `apps/server/config.json`, edit it, and mount/bind it when using Docker Compose (see `hosting/docker/docker-compose.yaml`).
2. For Helm, enable `colanode.configFile.enabled` and pass your file via `--set-file colanode.configFile.data=./config.json` (details in `hosting/kubernetes/README.md`).
3. Keep secrets as env vars so you don't have to bake them into JSON; the loader resolves `env://` pointers at runtime.

Environment variables no longer override regular config fields—only values explicitly tagged with `env://` are read from the environment. Refer to `hosting/docker/docker-compose.yaml` and `hosting/kubernetes/README.md` for mounting instructions and the handful of required secrets.

|`wal_enabled: bool`|Append mutations to the WAL. Disabling it permits process-crash data loss until a successful flush or close.|

|`memtable_size: usize`|Approximate in-memory byte threshold that triggers a memtable rotation and background flush.|

|`insert(key, value)`|Byte-like key and value|`Result<()>`. Inserts or replaces the key. The selected durability boundary is reached before success.|

|`insert_many(entries)`|Any iterator of `(key, value)` pairs|`Result<()>`. Copies the full iterator and applies entries in order; the last duplicate key wins. This is a bulk API, not one atomic visibility transition.|
|`get(key)`|Byte-like key|`Result<Option<Vec<u8>>>`. Returns `None` for missing or deleted keys and `Some(Vec::new())` for a stored empty value.|
|`remove(key)`|Byte-like key|`Result<()>`. Writes a tombstone; deleting a missing key is allowed.|

2. **SearchFacade replaces ElasticFacade.** Postgres full-text and JSON are the default backend; OpenSearch is optional. Plan: SearchFacade.
3. **qvt can be server-static.** With `server-static` set for `qvt`, the server sends a data-free compiled template and the client merges the data. Opt-in. Plan: QvtServerStatic.

4. **Print HTML is its own render mode.** `html-print` (print CSS and `@page`, also selected by the old `xsl-fo` name) is printed to PDF by one long-lived external Chromium; `/fop/<path>` sends a screen as PDF. Plan: Architecture-Proposal (Tool components and print).

5. **Cluster coordination uses the shared database.** Members find each other in a table; cache invalidation and notifications fan out over gRPC on client-certificate TLS (HTTP/1.1 POST as the alternative); no Hazelcast or Redis. Plan: Cluster.

6. **Sessions live in the database** (`moqui.server.HttpSession`, through the entity cache), with an optional guarantee mode so a load balancer without stickiness can fail over. Plan: Architecture-Proposal (Sessions and login).

7. **Keys are configuration, and unset secrets are generated.** Secrets are `default-property`s set by conf file or environment, never database rows; one still at its `CHANGEME` default is generated and saved to `runtime/.env`, which is loaded at startup like environment variables. Plan: MimoReview (Decisions 1–3).

8. **Feed registration commits with the entity change.** Search document keys are registered in the entity transaction; assembly and indexing run after commit, and an index failure does not roll back the change. Plan: SearchFacade.

**At a glance.** MIT licence. Python 3.11 or newer. Reads MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQLite, SQL Server, ClickHouse, Metabase and MongoDB, or `information_schema` dumps. Fifteen MCP tools: fourteen read-only and one that logs a query. Runs without a server, and the bundled demo webshop has 35 tables in three schemas. **The loop.** An agent that uses keygraph follows the same six steps for each question. The order is the one recommended in AGENTS.md.
Register the MCP server once and the fifteen tools appear in your agent (the configs for other clients are in MCP):
claude mcp add keygraph -- uvx --from 'keygraph[mcp]' keygraph mcp --dir /abs/path/to/out

The agent detects your database and its own harness, then asks you up to six questions. It builds the map, connects keygraph over MCP, and checks the result with `keygraph doctor`. Your credentials never go into a config file. Details are in setup/.

The build writes `graph.json`, `RELATIONS_REPORT.md`, `keygraph.html` (a self-contained explorer that works from disk, offline), `keygraph.db` (SQLite with full-text search) the agent pages `areas/*.md` and `tables/*.md`, and `build.json` (build time, keygraph version, source kind and database name, covered schemas; no host or credentials; the only file that differs between two identical builds, and `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` fixes its time). An unknown-table answer names the schemas the map covers. Details of every step are in How keygraph works (PDF) and examples/shop.

Grain, status codes, pitfalls and fan-out warnings come with the answers, which are the things a model otherwise has to guess. See AGENTS.md.

keygraph is a smaller tool with a narrower job. It reads an existing database and builds a map of keys, joins and business meaning as a folder of files. It does not define metrics for dashboards, transform data, track lineage, run a server or manage governance, which is what DataHub, OpenMetadata and similar catalogs are for (see the comparison). The metrics and status codes you record in keygraph's context file help search and agents, but keygraph does not compute them. This README does not compare keygraph with dbt or semantic-layer products feature by feature.

**What rich text holds.** Paragraphs, headings, bullet, numbered and task lists, quotes, code blocks, tables, horizontal rules and hard breaks; bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, subscript, superscript, inline code and links. A `relationship` node points at a document, a `block` node holds a row of any block type the field lists, and an `upload` node puts an image or a file in the flow (below). It's stored as a JSON tree:

- `text` links to the `pages` document whose slug is `install`. You can only name documents you can read; anything else gets the same 422 as a slug that doesn't exist. One write names at most 1,000 documents this way.

- `` on its own line is an upload node, or `media:<id>` when the field takes files from one collection. A node with fields is `::media:media/<id>{caption="Taken at dawn"}`, and one whose fields hold rich text takes a body, `:::media:media/<id>{…}` to `:::`. Only files already in TachyonCMS can be named, so an image pointing at a URL is refused.
- `<u>…</u>` is underline and ` ` (or ` `, ` `) is a hard break. That's all the HTML there is.

Markdown that doesn't fit is refused with a 422 and the line it's on, never half-converted: `line 3: raw HTML isn't allowed; the only tags are <u>…</u> and `, or ``line 3: unknown directive `:::aside` ``. A value can be up to 1 MiB, a numbered list starts at 1,000,000 at most, a NUL character is refused anywhere, and so is a directive straight after a task box (`- [ ] ::cta{…}`). Some things have no Markdown at all: subscript and superscript come out as plain text, and cell spans and `newTab` are dropped.
- A table cell holding several blocks, or one block that isn't a paragraph, becomes one paragraph, with ` ` between the blocks.

A link to a document goes to its collection's `url`, here `/{slug}`; without one, it's the link text alone. Block fields become `data-*` attributes (`ctaLabel` is `data-cta-label`), and anything that isn't a plain value is written as JSON. A relationship node is a ` ` around the linked document's first text field. Text is escaped, every `href` is checked again on the way out, and `newTab` links get `target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"`. As `text`, you get the words alone, the rich text inside block nodes included.

- **Link it.** An `upload` field links a post to its cover, with `filterOptions` to say which files fit. In rich text, an `upload` node is a ` ` in HTML, offering AVIF and WebP before the original, with its own fields as `data-*` attributes, and `alt` in Markdown. A field rule on any of a node's fields means whoever can't write that field can't replace text holding such a node either, the same as block nodes.

A few honest limits. A signed upload URL can't carry a size, so the size is checked when the document is created; set a size limit and lifecycle rules on the bucket, one for `_staging/` (older versions too, if versioning's on) and one to abort incomplete multipart uploads. Someone who can upload can tell that a filename they guess is taken, though not what holds it. Hiding `filename` with a field rule doesn't hide a file whose `sizes` they can still read. A file that isn't re-encoded keeps whatever its own format can hide inside its data, so set `formatOptions` when you need every image rewritten. Collections can't be deleted yet, so there's no file cleanup for that. Vercel Blob and Uploadthing will come as plugins. The uploads and storage docs cover the rest, every option included.
